subject: humanities
passage: In the margins of manuscripts made in northern Europe between about 1290 and 1340, an odd scene appears again and again: an armored knight confronting a snail. Sometimes the knight charges, sometimes he kneels in apparent surrender. Art historian Beatriz Olalde reads the motif as satire. A warrior cowering before the slowest creature imaginable mocks the pretensions of chivalry, and the joke would have landed with readers who knew knights mainly as a class that collected rents.
passage_b: The search for the one meaning of the snail knight may be misguided. The image appears in prayer books, legal texts, and romances, in England, France, and Flanders, drawn by dozens of artists over half a century. A motif that travels so far and lasts so long is best understood as a convention passed from workshop to workshop, a shape that illuminators enjoyed drawing, whose significance, if it ever had a single one, shifted with each hand that copied it. Asking what the snail means may be like asking what a doodle means.
stem: Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to the reading proposed by Olalde in Text 1?

choices.A: By agreeing that the images were meant to ridicule cowardly knights
choices.B: By arguing that the snail stands for a specific group that medieval writers mocked
choices.C: By suggesting that the motif's spread and variety make a single intended meaning unlikely
choices.D: By claiming that the images were drawn by a single artist over many years

explanation.why: Olalde reads the snail knight as a satire of chivalry. Text 2 says the search for "the one meaning" may be misguided, because the motif appears in many kinds of books, in several regions, by "dozens of artists over half a century," and so is better seen as a convention whose meaning "shifted with each hand." The author of Text 2 would respond that the motif's spread argues against any single intended meaning.
explanation.A: Incorrect. Text 2 does not endorse the satire reading; it questions whether any one reading fits.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Text 2 does not propose any specific target; it doubts that there is one.
explanation.C: Correct. Text 2 cites the motif's range of books, places, artists, and years as reasons to doubt a single meaning.
explanation.D: Incorrect. Text 2 says the images were drawn by "dozens of artists."
